# Bosun — Rails Deployment for Shared, Multi-Tenant Ubuntu Hosts

> Bosun is a `.deb`-packaged CLI for deploying Rails apps on
> [argus-tty](https://github.com/ramlaxmanyadav/argus-tty)-managed Ubuntu hosts. It solves a
> different problem than Capistrano/Mina/Kamal: not "how do I clone, build, and restart" (every tool
> answers that), but "how do several developers, a deployer, and an admin all deploy the same shared
> box without a common root account, without everyone's personal SSH key on the git host, and without
> every developer having standing read access to `DATABASE_URL`/`SECRET_KEY_BASE`."

Three enforced account tiers (developer/deployer/admin, via argus-tty, checked per-subcommand by
`require_role()`), secrets ACL-locked to a single unprivileged `webapp-svc` service account (not the
shared `webapps` group), one git deploy key per app distributed to every admin/deployer instead of N
personal keys, and a deploy pipeline (clone → bundle install → assets:precompile → symlink swap →
restart → health check → automatic rollback → cleanup) with zero new sudo privileges granted beyond
what argus-tty already whitelists.

argus-tty is recommended, not required: without it, bosun falls back to a single-operator
**standalone mode** automatically — no tiers, no separate service account, one account does
everything — see [standalone mode](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/standalone.html).

## Getting started

- [README](https://github.com/ramlaxmanyadav/bosun/blob/main/README.md): installing (Launchpad PPA
  or `.deb`) and a condensed quick start — the full reference lives in the docs below.
- [llms-full.txt](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/llms-full.txt): this file plus the complete
  content of the README and every `docs/*.md` file, concatenated into one fetch — for agents that
  prefer a single request over following links.
- [LICENSE](https://github.com/ramlaxmanyadav/bosun/blob/main/LICENSE): MIT.

## Documentation

- [installing](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/installing.html): Launchpad PPA (recommended,
  `ppa:yadavramlaxman/argus-tty` + `ppa:yadavramlaxman/bosun`) or the standalone `.deb` package,
  install order, verifying the install, and the standalone-mode fallback with no argus-tty.
- [walkthrough](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/walkthrough.html): the full walkthrough —
  setting up a new app from scratch, every command, real sample output.
- [permissions](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/permissions.html): who can do what — the
  developer/deployer/admin tier table, and why `shared/.env` is locked tighter than the rest of the
  app tree.
- [provisioning](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/provisioning.html): everything `bosun add`
  creates on disk — ACLs, `.env`, `deploy.conf`, systemd units, the git deploy key, RVM/gemsets — and
  why.
- [deploy-key](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/deploy-key.html): the shared, per-app git
  deploy key — one keypair distributed to every admin/deployer account, never developers, never a
  personal key.
- [running-commands](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/running-commands.html): `bosun run`
  (console/rake/migrations) and `bosun logs` — both load `shared/.env` the same way Puma/Sidekiq do.
- [customizing-deploy](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/customizing-deploy.html): overriding
  `do-release` with a full script instead of a hook DSL, for one app only.
- [custom-service](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/custom-service.html):
  adding a third service beyond the built-in Puma+Sidekiq pair (a sneakers/RabbitMQ consumer, Docker
  instead of systemd, anything else) in bosun's own format — the exec-wrapper pattern, the systemd
  unit template, and the one logging convention every bosun-managed worker follows.
- [systemd](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/systemd.html): exactly what
  `bosun add` generates for Puma/Sidekiq, the shipped reference `.service`/`.socket` samples, and
  optional socket activation.
- [crontab](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/crontab.html): the
  `/etc/cron.d/<app>` format bosun generates, why scheduled tasks must run as `webapp-svc`, and how to
  verify a job actually ran.
- [ruby-version](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/ruby-version.html):
  changing an app's Ruby version — the install/deploy sequence, and how old-version cleanup stays safe
  on a host where several apps share one RVM install.
- [standalone](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/standalone.html): running
  bosun without argus-tty — what single-operator standalone mode changes, the `/etc/bosun.conf`
  persisted-account file, and the security tradeoff it accepts.
- [nginx](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/nginx.html): reverse-proxying
  to the Puma unix socket (bosun doesn't manage nginx itself).

## Guides

- [Why bosun locks secrets to one service account instead of a shared group or box-wide env](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/secrets-locked-to-one-service-account.html):
  the ACL model behind `shared/.env`, and why there's no `dotenv-rails` dependency anywhere in the
  stack.
- [Multi-tenant Rails deployment: deploying without root or a personal SSH key](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/multi-tenant-rails-deployment.html):
  the developer/deployer/admin tier model and the shared per-app git deploy key, explained.
- [A full script override instead of a hook DSL](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/full-script-override-vs-hooks.html):
  why `do-release.sample` is plain bash you copy and edit, not a plugin system to learn, plus a
  worked example swapping Sidekiq for a RabbitMQ consumer.

## Quick start

```bash
# One time per host:
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yadavramlaxman/argus-tty && sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yadavramlaxman/bosun
sudo apt update && sudo apt install argus-tty bosun
sudo bosun bootstrap                   # installs RVM multi-user

# One time per app:
sudo bosun add myapp                   # provision /var/www/myapp, a shared deploy key, puma+sidekiq units
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/deploy.conf   # RUBY_VERSION, RUBY_GEMSET, PROJECT_REPO_URL
sudo vi /var/www/myapp/shared/.env     # DATABASE_URL, SECRET_KEY_BASE, RAILS_ENV
bosun install myapp                    # ruby/gemset + OS build deps
bosun setup myapp                      # releases/shared/config tree

# Every deploy after that:
bosun deploy myapp main
```

## Commands

- `sudo bosun add <app-name>` — provision an app (root only).
- `sudo bosun bootstrap` — RVM multi-user install, once per host (root only).
- `bosun install <app-name>` — ruby/gemset + OS build deps (developer/admin).
- `bosun setup <app-name>` — releases/shared/config tree (developer/admin).
- `bosun deploy <app-name> <git-branch>` — the actual deploy, with automatic rollback (deployer/admin).
- `bosun cleanup <app-name>` — prune old releases (deployer/admin; `deploy` also runs this
  automatically).
- `bosun restart <app-name>` — restart puma + sidekiq (deployer/admin).
- `bosun run <rails-args...> <app-name>` — any `rails` command/task, env loaded via `shared/bin/run`
  (developer/admin).
- `bosun logs [-t] <app-name>` — show or follow an app's Rails logs (developer/admin).
- `bosun mode [name]` — view or switch between argus-tty and standalone mode (view: any tier; set:
  root only).
- `bosun version [app-name]` — bosun's own version, RVM's version, and (given an app) its configured
  ruby/gemset — the one subcommand with no role restriction at all, since it exposes nothing
  sensitive.

## Links

- [GitHub repo](https://github.com/ramlaxmanyadav/bosun)
- [argus-tty](https://github.com/ramlaxmanyadav/argus-tty) (recommended — see the standalone doc for running without it)
- [This site's index](https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun/)


# Full documentation (concatenated)


# README.md

# bosun

Rails app deployment on top of [argus-tty](../argus-tty/)-managed hosts —
a **separate `.deb` package**, not nested inside argus-tty's repo (it's a
sibling directory). Its own `build-deb.sh`, its own `bosun` CLI, its own
`packaging/DEBIAN/control` declaring `Recommends: argus-tty` — optional,
not required; see [standalone mode](docs/standalone.md) below.

**Full documentation: https://ramlaxmanyadav.github.io/bosun** — the
complete command reference, the permission model, what `bosun add`
actually provisions, the shared deploy-key design, and every topic doc
below, all rendered in one place. This README covers installing and a
quick start only.

## Installing

Install order matters: argus-tty first (developer/admin accounts, the
sudoers whitelist, the `webapps`/`rvm` groups), then bosun on top.

### Option A — Launchpad PPA (recommended)

```bash
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yadavramlaxman/argus-tty
sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yadavramlaxman/bosun
sudo apt update
sudo apt install argus-tty bosun
```

Upgrades arrive via your regular `apt upgrade` instead of re-downloading a
`.deb` by hand. See [argus-tty/PACKAGING.md](../argus-tty/PACKAGING.md) if
you want to build and publish your own PPA instead of using these.

### Option B — the `.deb` package

```bash
sudo apt install ./argus-tty_1.0.0_all.deb
sudo apt install ./bosun_1.0.0_all.deb
```

Verify both landed correctly before provisioning any app:

```bash
sudo argus-tty status   # confirm green
bosun version           # confirms `bosun` resolves its own helper scripts at all —
                         # failing here means the .deb didn't lay files down where
                         # `bosun` expects them to be
```

bosun's own scripts (`add.sh`, `install`, `setup`, `do-release`,
`release-cleanup`, `bootstrap`) source argus-tty's installed
`/usr/lib/argus-tty/lib/common.sh` directly for the constants/helpers they
need (`AT_WEBAPPS_ROOT`, `AT_WEBAPPS_GROUP`, `AT_RVM_ROOT`,
`AT_WEBAPPS_SVC_USER`, `require_root`, `valid_username`, `info`/`warn`/
`error`) — a real cross-package dependency, not just a doc note.

**No argus-tty?** Bosun falls back to a single-operator **standalone mode**
instead of refusing to run — no tiers, no separate service account, every
secret only as isolated as your one account's own permissions. This also
works the other way: `sudo bosun mode standalone`/`argus-tty` lets you
choose explicitly regardless of what's installed — force standalone on a
box that happens to have argus-tty too, or require argus-tty strictly so
bosun errors instead of silently degrading if it's ever removed by
accident. Switching modes never touches an existing app's code or
`shared/.env` content — see [docs/standalone.md](docs/standalone.md) for
the full tradeoff and the exact `bosun add`/`bosun restart` steps to apply
a mode switch to apps already deployed.

Every developer, admin, and deployer account (managed by argus-tty) is
automatically a member of a shared `webapps` group (and of `rvm`, if RVM is
already installed on the box) — see argus-tty's `add-developer.sh`. This is
what lets them create and edit application files without any sudo access, on
top of argus-tty's existing whitelist model.

## Quick start

```bash
# One-time per host
sudo bosun bootstrap                   # installs RVM multi-user AND retrofits existing accounts + webapp-svc onto webapps/rvm

# One-time per app
sudo bosun add myapp                   # provision /var/www/myapp, a shared deploy key, puma+sidekiq units
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/deploy.conf   # RUBY_VERSION, RUBY_GEMSET, PROJECT_REPO_URL
sudo vi /var/www/myapp/shared/.env     # DATABASE_URL, SECRET_KEY_BASE, RAILS_ENV
bosun install myapp                    # ruby/gemset + OS build deps
bosun setup myapp                      # releases/shared/config tree

# Every deploy after that
bosun deploy myapp main
```

Full walkthrough — real account onboarding, the deploy-key handoff, sample
output at every step — in [docs/walkthrough.md](docs/walkthrough.md).

# docs/walkthrough.md

# Walkthrough: setting up a new app from scratch

One-time per host (skip if already done; see the [README](../README.md#installing)
for the Launchpad PPA option):

```bash
sudo apt install ./argus-tty_1.0.0_all.deb    # or sudo ./install.sh from a loose checkout, or the PPA (see the README)
sudo apt install ./bosun_1.0.0_all.deb
sudo argus-tty status                          # confirm green

sudo bosun bootstrap                # installs RVM multi-user AND retrofits existing accounts + webapp-svc onto webapps/rvm
```

One-time per app:

```bash
# 1. Admin: provision the app
sudo bosun add myapp
# Prints a public key — add it as a read-only Deploy Key on myapp's git
# repo (see docs/deploy-key.md). Already distributed to every current
# developer/admin account, so no per-person git access to set up.

# If the deploying developer has no account yet:
sudo argus-tty add alice --name "Alice Kumar" --pubkey alice_id_ed25519.pub
# (they must log out/in if they were already logged in — group membership
# doesn't apply retroactively to an open session)
# Since they were just added, backfill their copy of myapp's deploy key:
sudo bosun add myapp
```

```bash
# 2. Developer: fill in deploy metadata
ssh alice@host
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/deploy.conf
#   RUBY_VERSION=ruby-3.3.3
#   RUBY_GEMSET=myapp
#   PROJECT_REPO_URL=git@git.example.com:yourorg/myapp.git
#   KEEP_LATEST_RELEASE=5

# 3. Admin: fill in app secrets — shared/.env is root:root 600 (ACL read
#    grant for webapp-svc only), so a developer/deployer account can't
#    open it directly even to overwrite it; only an admin's full sudo
#    covers this (see docs/permissions.md).
sudo vi /var/www/myapp/shared/.env
#   DATABASE_URL=postgres://...
#   SECRET_KEY_BASE=...
#   RAILS_ENV=production

# 4. Developer: install this app's Ruby + OS build deps
#    What this actually does (deployment/install): installs the OS packages
#    Rails native gems need (nodejs, libmysqlclient-dev, imagemagick, etc. —
#    sudo apt-get, whitelisted for developers), then `rvm install` +
#    `rvm use --create` for the RUBY_VERSION@RUBY_GEMSET from step 2's
#    deploy.conf, then `gem install bundler`. No sudo needed for the RVM
#    part — multi-user RVM is group-writable. Requires `bosun bootstrap`
#    (above) to have already run once on this host.
bosun install myapp
# [INFO]  Installing OS build dependencies (sudo apt-get — whitelisted for developers)...
# [INFO]  Installing ruby-3.3.3 (gemset: myapp) via RVM — no sudo needed, multi-user RVM is group-writable...
# [INFO]  Dependencies installed for 'myapp': ruby-3.3.3@myapp + bundler.
bosun version myapp   # sanity-check: confirms the ruby/gemset deploy.conf actually has on file

# 5. Developer: set up the shared config tree — run from a checkout of the
#    APP's own repo (puma.rb/secret.yml templates are copied from ./ ).
#    What this actually does (deployment/setup): creates releases/shared/
#    config/log/tmp under /var/www/myapp, writes shared/.ruby-version +
#    .ruby-gemset (so RVM's cd-hook auto-selects the right ruby the moment
#    anyone `cd`s into current/), and copies ./puma.rb + ./secret.yml from
#    the repo checkout you're running it from into shared/config/. Idempotent
#    — safe to re-run; it never overwrites a database.yml/sidekiq.yml/
#    secret.yml that already has real content in it, so a second run after
#    you've filled those in won't blow your edits away.
git clone git@git.example.com:yourorg/myapp.git /tmp/myapp-config
cd /tmp/myapp-config
bosun setup myapp
# Project directory setup started for 'myapp'...
# [WARN]  ./secret.yml not found in /tmp/myapp-config — skipping (expected to come from the app repo checkout).
# Please fill in /var/www/myapp/shared/config/database.yml/sidekiq.yml/sidekiq.rb for 'myapp'.
# App secrets (DATABASE_URL, SECRET_KEY_BASE, etc.) belong in /var/www/myapp/shared/.env, not in a config file.
# [INFO]  Setup complete for 'myapp'.
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/config/database.yml
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/config/sidekiq.yml
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/config/sidekiq.rb

# 6. Developer: first deploy
bosun deploy myapp main
```

Verify:

```bash
sudo systemctl status puma-myapp sidekiq-myapp
sudo journalctl -u puma-myapp -n 50
```

Need a console or to run a migration by hand afterward? Don't invoke
`bundle`/`rails` directly — use `bosun run` so `shared/.env` is
actually loaded (see [docs/running-commands.md](running-commands.md)):

```bash
bosun run console myapp
bosun run db:migrate myapp
```

Steps 1–5 are one-time per app. Every deploy after that is just step 6 again:
`bosun deploy myapp <branch>`. Want to prune old releases outside of a
deploy? `bosun cleanup myapp` (runs automatically at the end of
every `deploy` anyway).

# docs/permissions.md

# Who can do what (account tiers)

argus-tty has three account tiers; bosun enforces which of its own
subcommands each one can run (`require_role()` in `deployment/lib/common`,
checked against the caller's *active* session groups):

| Command                    | developer | deployer | admin |
|-----------------------------|:---------:|:--------:|:-----:|
| `add` (provision an app)    | —         | —        | root only |
| `bootstrap` (RVM, one time)  | —         | —        | root only |
| `install` / `setup`         | ✓         | —        | ✓     |
| `run` (console/rake) / `logs` | ✓       | —        | ✓     |
| `deploy` / `cleanup`        | —         | ✓        | ✓     |
| `systemctl start/stop/restart` (via sudo) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `version` (bosun/RVM/app version info) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| `mode` (view)                | ✓         | ✓        | ✓     |
| `mode <name>` (set)          | —         | —        | root only |

A plain developer can't deploy; a plain deployer can't open a console, run
rake, install deps, or tail logs. `version` and `mode` (viewing it) are the
two exceptions with no `require_role()` gate at all — neither exposes
anything sensitive (bosun's own version, RVM's version, an app's
`deploy.conf` ruby/gemset; the configured/effective mode), so every tier
can run them freely. Setting a mode (`sudo bosun mode <name>`) writes to
`/etc/bosun.conf`, so that part is root-only regardless of tier. This whole
table only applies when argus-tty is actually installed — in
[standalone mode](standalone.md) `require_role()` always passes,
since there's only one account to enforce tiers against in the first
place. Sudoers only covers the root-requiring
parts (`systemctl`, `apt-get`, `docker`) — the actual file access
(clone/bundle install/symlink/console) is plain Unix permissions under the
`webapps` group, which is why bosun's own `require_role()` check exists:
without it, anyone in `webapps` could run any subcommand regardless of
their argus-tty tier.

`shared/.env` (app secrets) is a stricter boundary still: it's readable by
root and, via a single named-user ACL grant, the `webapp-svc` service
account only — **not** the `webapps` group, so developer and deployer
accounts can't read or edit it directly even though they're both `webapps`
members. Admin edits it with `sudo vi shared/.env` (full sudo already
covers this, no extra grant needed). A developer still gets a **working**
`bosun run console myapp` with real secrets loaded: `run` elevates to
`webapp-svc` via a narrowly-scoped sudoers grant (`sudo -u webapp-svc`,
exact path only) instead of reading the file as themselves.

# docs/provisioning.md

# Provisioning an app (`bosun add`)

```bash
sudo bosun add myapp     # one-time per app, run as root/sudo
```

This provisions `/var/www/myapp` with:
- **setgid (`2775`)** on every directory, so new files/dirs are owned by the
  `webapps` group regardless of which developer created them.
- A **default ACL** (`setfacl -d -m g:webapps:rwX`) granting the group
  effective write access on anything created inside, independent of the
  `umask 027` that argus-tty's `profile.d/developer-restrictions.sh` already
  applies to every developer/admin login — without that ACL, umask 027
  would strip the group-write bit and one developer couldn't edit another's
  files.
- `/var/www/myapp/shared/.env` — an empty, `600` `root:root` file for this
  app's env vars (`DATABASE_URL`, `SECRET_KEY_BASE`, etc.), plus a single
  named-user ACL read grant for `webapp-svc`. Deliberately **not**
  `webapps`-group readable — see [permissions.md](permissions.md) for why,
  and edit it with `sudo vi /var/www/myapp/shared/.env`.
- `/var/www/myapp/shared/deploy.conf` — `660`, holds `RUBY_VERSION`,
  `RUBY_GEMSET`, `PROJECT_REPO_URL`, `KEEP_LATEST_RELEASE` (deploy-pipeline
  metadata, not a secret — that's `.env` above). Read by every deploy
  subcommand. Also where you can optionally set `RELEASE_VERSION_CMD` to
  override how `deploy` names each release — unset, it's a plain timestamp
  (unchanged default); e.g. `RELEASE_VERSION_CMD='echo "$(date
  +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)"'` makes releases traceable to
  a commit instead. Runs with the freshly cloned repo as its working
  directory, so `git` commands resolve.
- `shared/bin/{puma,sidekiq}-exec` — small wrapper scripts that resolve
  `RUBY_VERSION@RUBY_GEMSET` from `deploy.conf` at *run* time via RVM's
  per-gemset wrapper scripts, so the systemd units below never need editing
  when a developer bumps the ruby version.
- `shared/bin/run` — the same env-loading, but forwards arbitrary args
  instead of a fixed command: `shared/bin/run rails console`, `shared/bin/run
  rake db:migrate`. Use this for anything run by hand instead of invoking
  `bundle`/`rails` directly — see "Why a per-app `.env` file" below for why
  it exists instead of a gem.
- `shared/.ruby-version` / `shared/.ruby-gemset` (symlinked into `current/`
  by `deploy`) — RVM's cd-hook auto-loads `RUBY_VERSION@RUBY_GEMSET` the
  moment you `cd` into `current/` interactively, with **no trust prompt**.
  Deliberately **not** a `.rvmrc` (RVM's older mechanism): `.rvmrc` is
  arbitrary shell code RVM has to ask you to trust the first time — real
  interactive-login friction — and this toolkit's own `.rvmrc` used to also
  `source shared/.env` as whoever `cd`'d in, which would silently reopen the
  exact access `.env`'s permissions now deny developer/deployer accounts
  (see [permissions.md](permissions.md)). Not generated at all anymore.
- `puma-myapp.service` / `sidekiq-myapp.service` — installed under
  `/etc/systemd/system/`, enabled but not started (there's no release yet).
  Run as `webapp-svc`, an unprivileged, no-login system account — not root,
  not a developer's own account. Developers start/stop/restart these via
  argus-tty's already-whitelisted `systemctl {start,stop,restart} *` sudoers
  entry; they have no way to create or edit unit files themselves, by
  design — only `add` (run by an admin) does that.
- `shared/deploy_key` / `shared/deploy_key.pub` — a git deploy keypair
  generated once for this app and distributed to every current
  developer/admin account, so `deploy` can `git clone` without anyone using
  their own personal SSH key. See [deploy-key.md](deploy-key.md).

**Existing accounts** created before this feature: `bosun add` (first app
on a box), `bosun bootstrap`, and `argus-tty add`/`add-admin`/`add-deployer`
all retrofit every current developer/admin/deployer account onto
`webapps`/`rvm` automatically now — no separate `sudo argus-tty
reconfigure` step needed just for this. An account with an **already-open**
session still needs a fresh login to pick up new group membership (a PAM
limit, not something any script can work around).

**Why a per-app `.env` file instead of the box-wide `/etc/environment`:**
`/etc/environment` is sourced into *every* login shell and PAM session on the
host — including admins'. Any sudoers rule broad enough to let developers
edit it (even a "restricted" wrapper) is a realistic path to tampering with
root's environment (`LD_PRELOAD`, `BASH_ENV`, arbitrary vars) on next login —
a bigger hole than argus-tty's whitelist model is designed to allow.
`shared/.env` confines each app's secrets to that app's own directory
permissions instead — and, on top of that, its own permissions are tighter
than the rest of the app tree (root + a named-user ACL grant for
`webapp-svc` only, not the `webapps` group — see [permissions.md](permissions.md)):
even a compromised or malicious developer/deployer account has no standing
read access to it at all.

`add`/`do-release` wire this up with no gem dependency (deliberately not
`dotenv-rails` — a plain `.env` file does nothing on its own without
something to read it, and we didn't want that something to be a Gemfile
addition every app has to carry): the `puma-<app>`/`sidekiq-<app>` systemd
units load it via `EnvironmentFile=-shared/.env` (read by root, so `.env`'s
tight permissions don't matter there), and, redundantly, the `puma-exec`/
`sidekiq-exec` wrapper scripts also `source` it before exec'ing — they run
as `webapp-svc`, which has the ACL grant. For anything run by hand —
`rails console`, `rake`, migrations — use `bosun run` (e.g.
`bosun run console myapp`) instead of invoking `bundle`/`rails` directly;
it elevates to `webapp-svc` to load the same `deploy.conf`/`shared/.env`
before running whatever command you pass it, without requiring the calling
developer/admin's own account to read `.env` directly.

**RVM / gemsets:** this toolkit does not install RVM as part of `add` —
run `sudo bosun bootstrap` once per host instead (root, one-time;
see [walkthrough.md](walkthrough.md)). It installs RVM in
[multi-user mode](https://rvm.io/rvm/install) (a system-wide `/usr/local/rvm`
and an `rvm` group). Once that group exists, every developer/admin/deployer account
(new, or retrofitted automatically by `bootstrap` itself) is added to it
automatically — as is the `webapp-svc` service account, which also needs
`rvm` membership to actually load the gems it runs — so
`ruby`/`bundle`/`rails`/gemset commands work with no sudo needed.

`bootstrap` also cleans up conflicting **per-user** RVM installs every
time it runs (not just on first install) — e.g. `~ubuntu/.rvm` from someone
having run RVM's installer directly on some account before this toolkit's
multi-user `/usr/local/rvm` existed. A per-user install auto-loads via a
line in that account's `.bashrc`/`.bash_profile`, and RVM's own scripts
aren't safe to load twice — the symptom is a login (or anything with a
login-shell shebang) crashing with `... unbound variable` (e.g.
`rvm_bash_nounset` or `_system_name`), which has nothing to do with
whatever command happened to trigger it. `bootstrap` finds every
`/home/*/.rvm` and `/root/.rvm`, strips the auto-load line from that
account's shell rc files, and leaves the actual `.rvm` directory in place
(never auto-deletes gemset data) — remove it yourself once you've confirmed
nothing still depends on it.

# docs/deploy-key.md

# Git deploy key (shared, not personal)

`deploy` needs to `git clone` each app's repo, which normally means SSH
access to that repo. Rather than every admin/deployer using their own
personal key (which means whitelisting N different keys in your git host,
and losing access the moment someone's personal key rotates or they're
offboarded), `add` generates **one dedicated keypair per app** and
distributes it to every current admin/deployer account automatically:

```bash
sudo bosun add myapp
# ── Generated git deploy key for 'myapp' ──
# Add this PUBLIC key as a Deploy Key on 'myapp's git repo (e.g. GitLab:
# Project > Settings > Repository > Deploy Keys) — read-only is enough,
# 'deploy' only ever clones:
#
# ssh-ed25519 AAAA... bosun@myapp
#
# Distributed 'myapp' deploy key to 2 admin/deployer account(s).
```

What to do with the printed public key: add it as a **Deploy Key** on the
app's repo (GitLab: *Project → Settings → Repository → Deploy Keys*; GitHub:
*Settings → Deploy keys*) — read-only access is enough, `deploy` never
pushes. One deploy key per repo, shared by everyone allowed to deploy that
app (deployer/admin — see [permissions.md](permissions.md)); add/remove people from
the `admin`/`deployer` groups (argus-tty) to control who can, not the git
host's key list.

**Developer deliberately never gets a copy of this key.** `require_role()`
already blocks a plain developer from running `deploy` at all — handing
them a personal, readable copy of the app's git deploy key anyway would be
pure unnecessary exposure, especially if that key is also what a GitLab CI
pipeline uses (via a dedicated deployer account) to trigger deploys
remotely. `add` actively removes any copy a developer account received
under an older version that didn't make this distinction.

Where it lives:
- **Private key**: `/var/www/myapp/shared/deploy_key` (`600`, `root:root` —
  nobody can read the private key file directly, even though deployer/admin
  accounts can use it via `deploy`).
- **Distributed copies**: `~/.ssh/bosun/myapp/id_ed25519`, one
  individually-owned `600` copy in *every* current admin/deployer account's
  own home directory (never developer's — see above) — `deploy`
  (`do-release`) picks this up automatically via `GIT_SSH_COMMAND` when it
  exists, falling back to that account's own default SSH setup (with a
  warning) if it doesn't.

Re-running `add myapp` on an existing app leaves an already-generated
key untouched and just re-distributes it — safe to re-run any time (e.g.
after onboarding a new admin/deployer, to backfill their copy without
regenerating the key or re-whitelisting anything in GitLab). Onboard anyone
*after* `add` already ran once for an app? Re-run
`sudo bosun add myapp` for each such app to distribute that app's
key to the new account (this doesn't touch anything already provisioned —
`.env`, `deploy.conf`, systemd units, etc. are all left exactly as they are).

# docs/running-commands.md

# Running rails commands and tailing logs

`bosun run` is a generic wrapper around `rails` for one app — console,
migrations, a custom rake task, `rails runner`, anything listed by `rails -T`
— not a fixed list of shortcuts. The **app name is the last argument**
(everything before it forwards to `rails` verbatim, including its own
flags), unlike `install`/`setup`/`deploy`/`cleanup`, which take
the app name first:

```bash
bosun run console myapp                          # -> bundle exec rails console
bosun run db:migrate myapp                        # -> bundle exec rails db:migrate
bosun run db:migrate VERSION=20260101120000 myapp  # extra args forward too
bosun run runner 'puts User.count' myapp           # quote multi-word args as one
```

No sudo, no gem dependency, and it never touches `bundle`/`rails` directly
itself — it resolves the app's `shared/bin/run` wrapper (created by
`add`) and execs `rails "$@"` through it, so `RUBY_VERSION`/
`RUBY_GEMSET`/`deploy.conf`/`shared/.env` are loaded exactly the same way
`puma`/`sidekiq` get them.

`bosun logs` shows (or follows) an app's Rails log files under
`shared/log/` — the same directory `current/log` symlinks to. No sudo
needed; `shared/` is already `webapps`-group readable for every developer/
admin account:

```bash
bosun logs myapp        # last 200 lines, then exit
bosun logs -t myapp     # follow (like tail -f), Ctrl-C to stop
```

This is the app's own `Rails.logger` output (`log/production.log`, etc.) —
for the puma/sidekiq *process's* stdout/stderr (crashes, boot errors before
Rails.logger even starts), use `sudo journalctl -u puma-myapp` /
`-u sidekiq-myapp` instead — already whitelisted for developers, no
argument restriction.

# docs/customizing-deploy.md

# Customizing deploy for one app

The built-in `deploy` (do-release) manages exactly puma + sidekiq for every
app, unconditionally — no config knob to learn for the common case. If one
specific app needs something different (a different background worker like
[sneakers](https://github.com/jondot/sneakers) instead of Sidekiq, extra
build steps, a health check, whatever), override the whole script instead of
configuring around the edges:

```bash
cp /usr/lib/bosun/deploy/do-release.sample /var/www/myapp/shared/do-release
chmod +x /var/www/myapp/shared/do-release
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/do-release        # it's your script now, edit freely
```

`bosun deploy myapp <branch>` checks for `shared/do-release` first
and, if it's present and executable, runs *that* instead of the built-in
default — for `myapp` only, every other app on the box keeps using the
default untouched. Copied-and-unedited it behaves identically to the
built-in default, so the first useful step after copying it is deploying
once with no changes, to confirm the override wiring itself works before
customizing.

If an app has **no** override at all (or one that exists but isn't
executable — e.g. someone forgot the `chmod +x` above), `deploy` doesn't
fail or block: it prints a one-line, non-blocking warning to that effect
and proceeds with the built-in puma+sidekiq default. This is just a safety
net so a missing/mistyped override is visible in the deploy's own output
instead of silently falling back with no trace — most apps are expected to
never need an override at all. See
[custom-service.md](custom-service.md) for adding a third
service this way.

This is a full script replacement, not a hook, so it can do anything a
whitelisted developer/admin already can — different `systemctl` units, or
run a worker via `docker` instead of systemd entirely (already fully
whitelisted, and sidesteps the fact that developers have no way to create
new unit files themselves). `do-release.sample`'s comments walk through both
options for the "swap Sidekiq for a sneakers worker" example. What it can't
do is grant new privileges — every `sudo` call in your override is still
checked against the exact same developer/admin sudoers whitelist as
everything else in argus-tty; writing your own script doesn't add to it.

# docs/custom-service.md

# Adding a custom service (beyond puma + sidekiq)

`sudo bosun add <app-name>` only ever generates two systemd units:
`puma-<app>.service` and `sidekiq-<app>.service` (see
[systemd.md](systemd.md)). Some apps need a third long-running process — a
RabbitMQ consumer ([sneakers](https://github.com/jondot/sneakers)), a
different queue backend, a scheduled worker pool, whatever. This doc covers
how to add one **in bosun's own format**, so it gets the same env loading,
logging convention, and deploy-time start/stop handling every other
bosun-managed process already gets, instead of a one-off hand-rolled unit
that drifts from everything else on the box.

> **Standalone mode (no argus-tty):** `User=webapp-svc Group=webapps` in
> the template below is actually `User=<your account> Group=bosun-apps` —
> match whatever `/etc/bosun.conf`/the puma/sidekiq units on your host
> already use. See [standalone.md](standalone.md).

## Why this isn't self-service the way `install`/`setup` are

Developers/admins have no whitelisted way to create or edit systemd unit
files themselves (no `sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/...` in argus-tty's
sudoers whitelist, by design — see [permissions.md](permissions.md)).
`bosun add`'s `write_unit()` is the only thing that creates unit files, and
it only ever calls itself for `puma`/`sidekiq`. That leaves two paths for a
third service:

- **Ask an admin to hand-create the unit** (below) — still fully
  whitelisted work (`systemctl start/stop/restart/status` already is), just
  not something `bosun add` does automatically for you.
- **Run it via `docker` instead** — already fully whitelisted for
  developers/admins, no unit file needed at all. See "Docker instead of
  systemd" below.

Either way, your app's own deploy override (`shared/do-release`) is what
actually starts/stops/restarts it on every deploy — see "Wiring it into
deploy" below.

## Path 1: a hand-created systemd unit

Ask an admin to create `/etc/systemd/system/<name>-<app>.service`, following
**exactly** the same template `bin/add.sh`'s `write_unit()` uses for
puma/sidekiq — same user, same env loading, same restart policy:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=<name> (<app>)
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=webapp-svc
Group=webapps
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/<app>/current
EnvironmentFile=-/var/www/<app>/shared/.env
ExecStart=/var/www/<app>/shared/bin/<name>-exec
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=3

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable <name>-<app>.service   # don't start yet — no exec wrapper exists until the next step
```

### The exec wrapper (`shared/bin/<name>-exec`) — this part IS self-service

Unlike the unit file, `shared/bin/` is `webapps`-group writable — any
developer/admin can create this without an admin's help, same as `bosun
add` already does for `shared/bin/puma-exec`/`shared/bin/sidekiq-exec`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# shared/bin/<name>-exec — resolves RUBY_VERSION/RUBY_GEMSET from
# deploy.conf at RUN time, not template time, same as puma-exec/
# sidekiq-exec.
set -euo pipefail
set -a
source "/var/www/<app>/shared/deploy.conf"
[[ -f "/var/www/<app>/shared/.env" ]] && source "/var/www/<app>/shared/.env"
set +a
cd "/var/www/<app>/current"
# RVM's wrapper binaries don't set rvm_path themselves — without it, RVM's
# stock per-ruby .irbrc falls through to requiring a personal ~/irbrc that
# usually doesn't exist, crashing irb/console for everyone.
export rvm_path="/usr/local/rvm"
# Own logfile via shell redirection (>> ... 2>&1) — NOT systemd's
# StandardOutput=file:/StandardError=file:, and NOT a `-L`/`--logfile` CLI
# flag if the process doesn't have one (Sidekiq 6.0+ removed its own
# entirely). This is the one logging convention every bosun-managed
# worker uses — see the sidekiq-exec/sneaker-exec wrappers for other apps
# in this repo's scripts/ directory that already do this.
exec "/usr/local/rvm/wrappers/${RUBY_VERSION}@${RUBY_GEMSET}/bundle" exec <your-command-here> \
  >> "/var/www/<app>/shared/log/<name>.log" 2>&1
```

```bash
chmod 755 /var/www/<app>/shared/bin/<name>-exec
sudo systemctl start <name>-<app>.service
tail -f /var/www/<app>/shared/log/<name>.log
```

### Worked example: a sneakers (RabbitMQ) consumer

```bash
# unit: sneaker-myapp.service — ExecStart=/var/www/myapp/shared/bin/sneaker-exec
# shared/bin/sneaker-exec's exec line:
exec "/usr/local/rvm/wrappers/${RUBY_VERSION}@${RUBY_GEMSET}/bundle" exec rake sneakers:run \
  >> "/var/www/myapp/shared/log/sneaker.log" 2>&1
```

If the worker needs its own fixed config (which queue, concurrency) rather
than a secret, bake it in as a plain `export` in the wrapper, same as
`-q`/`-c` flags get baked into a `sidekiq-<name>-exec` wrapper — it isn't a
secret, so it doesn't belong in `shared/.env`:

```bash
export WORKERS="GhaProcessQueueWorker"
export RM_WORKER="4"
```

## Path 2: Docker instead of systemd

No unit file, no admin needed — `docker` is already fully whitelisted:

```bash
sudo docker rm -f <name>-<app> 2>/dev/null || true
sudo docker run -d --name <name>-<app> --restart unless-stopped \
  -v "/var/www/<app>/current:/app" -w /app --env-file "/var/www/<app>/shared/.env" \
  your-ruby-image bundle exec <your-command-here>
```

Your deploy override then calls `docker stop|start|inspect <name>-<app>`
wherever the systemd path below calls `systemctl`/`svc_active`.

## Wiring it into deploy

The built-in `do-release` only knows about `puma-<app>`/`sidekiq-<app>`. A
third service needs a per-app override — copy `do-release.sample` to
`/var/www/<app>/shared/do-release`, `chmod +x` it, and:

1. Rename every `*_worker` function/variable to your service's name (e.g.
   `WORKER_UNIT` -> `SNEAKER_UNIT`, matching the unit name from Path 1, or
   the container name from Path 2).
2. Swap the `systemctl stop/start`/`svc_active` calls in those renamed
   functions for `docker stop/start/inspect` if you went with Path 2.
3. Deploy once with no other changes first, to confirm the override and
   the new service both actually come up, before customizing further.

See `do-release.sample`'s own header comment for the exact lines to touch
— it already documents this swap in detail. `deployment/do-release` (the
built-in default) now also prints a one-line, non-blocking warning on
every deploy for an app with no override at all, as a safety net against a
forgotten or mistyped `shared/do-release` — see its own comment.

## Logging — the one rule every custom service should follow

Own logfile via shell redirection in the exec wrapper (`>> logfile 2>&1`),
not systemd's `StandardOutput=file:`/`StandardError=file:` and not a
process's own `-L`/`--logfile` flag if it has one. Three reasons this is
the standard across every bosun-managed worker:

- A process-level flag might not exist (Sidekiq 6.0+ removed `-L`/`-P`/`-d`
  entirely — it expects an external supervisor, i.e. systemd, to own
  logging).
- `StandardOutput=file:` opens the file as root before systemd drops
  privileges to `webapp-svc` — if the process later reopens that same path
  itself (as Puma does for `config/puma.rb`'s own `stdout_redirect`), the
  reopen fails with `EACCES` because the file's now root-owned. See
  [systemd.md](systemd.md)'s note on exactly this for Puma.
- One convention, one place to look, regardless of which process it is —
  `tail -f shared/log/<name>.log` always works the same way.

# docs/systemd.md

# systemd units: puma + sidekiq

`sudo bosun add <app-name>` writes and enables two systemd units per app
automatically — you normally never write one by hand. This doc covers what
gets generated, the shipped reference copies, and optional socket
activation.

> **Standalone mode (no argus-tty):** `User=webapp-svc Group=webapps`
> below is actually `User=<your account> Group=bosun-apps` — the generated
> units already have the right names for your host. See
> [standalone.md](standalone.md).

## What `bosun add` generates

`write_unit()` in `bin/add.sh` writes both units directly (not from a
template file):

```
/etc/systemd/system/puma-<app>.service
/etc/systemd/system/sidekiq-<app>.service
```

Both run as `User=webapp-svc Group=webapps`, `WorkingDirectory=<app>/current`,
`EnvironmentFile=-<app>/shared/.env`, `Restart=on-failure`. They're
`enable`d but not started by `add` — there's no release yet
(`current` doesn't exist until the first `bosun deploy`).

Restart both at once with `bosun restart <app-name>` (added alongside this
doc — admin/deployer tier, same as `deploy`/`cleanup`), or individually via
the already-whitelisted `sudo systemctl {start,stop,restart} <unit>`.

## The shipped reference copies

Two files ship at `/usr/lib/bosun/deploy/`:

- `puma-app_name.service.sample` — an annotated copy of what `bosun add`
  already generates. Useful as a reference, or to hand-create a unit
  outside the normal `bosun add` flow.
- `puma-app_name.socket.sample` — optional socket-activation unit (see
  below).

Both are templates with the literal placeholder `app_name` — replace every
occurrence with your actual app name before using either by hand.

**Puma's own log redirect, and why the generated unit doesn't also
redirect stdout/stderr:** `config/puma.rb` (the app's own file) already
does its own `stdout_redirect` to `shared/log/puma.log`. If the systemd
unit also set `StandardOutput=`/`StandardError=` to that same path, systemd
would create/open it as root before dropping privileges to
`User=webapp-svc`, and Puma's later reopen of that now-root-owned file
would fail with `EACCES`. Leave those unset (defaults to the journal) and
let Puma own the file itself. Unit-level events (start/stop/restart,
failures to launch) still show up in the journal regardless:

```bash
sudo journalctl -t puma-<app> -f
```

## Socket activation (optional)

`puma-app_name.socket.sample` lets systemd own the Unix socket file
(`shared/tmp/sockets/puma.sock`) and hand Puma an already-open file
descriptor, instead of Puma creating/binding the socket itself at boot.
Buys zero dropped connections across a Puma restart. To use it:

1. Copy `puma-app_name.socket.sample` to
   `/etc/systemd/system/puma-<app>.socket`, replacing `app_name`.
2. **Remove or comment out** the `bind "unix://..."` line in the app's
   `config/puma.rb` — with socket activation, systemd owns that path; Puma
   trying to bind it too defeats the point (and can fail outright).
3. Add `Requires=puma-<app>.socket` under `[Unit]` in
   `puma-<app>.service` so the socket is always up before Puma starts.
4. `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`
5. `sudo systemctl enable --now puma-<app>.socket` (starting just the
   `.socket` activates on first connection; start both units if you don't
   need on-demand activation).

This is entirely optional — `config/puma.rb` binding its own socket
directly (the default `bosun add` leaves in place) is simpler and fine for
most setups; socket activation only matters if dropped connections during
a Puma restart are a real concern for this app.

# docs/crontab.md

# Scheduled tasks: `/etc/cron.d/<app>`

`sudo bosun add <app-name>` writes `/etc/cron.d/<app-name>` automatically —
fully commented out, so it has zero effect until you edit it. This doc
covers the format, why it must run as `webapp-svc`, and how to confirm a
job actually ran.

> **Standalone mode (no argus-tty):** every `webapp-svc` below is actually
> whatever account `/etc/bosun.conf` names (see
> [standalone.md](standalone.md)) — the cron file `bosun add` generates
> already has the right name baked in for your host, so copy its own
> example line rather than the literal `webapp-svc` shown here.

## The file `bosun add` generates

```
# /etc/cron.d/myapp — scheduled tasks for 'myapp'.
#
# cron.d format has 6 fields, NOT 5 like a personal 'crontab -e':
#   min hour dom month dow  user  command
#
# Run as 'webapp-svc' — the same unprivileged account puma/sidekiq already
# run as. It's the only account with a read grant on shared/.env, so any
# scheduled task that needs real app env vars loaded must run as this user
# via the generated shared/bin/run wrapper, not as root or a developer
# account.
#
# Example (uncomment and edit — runs daily at 02:30):
#30 2 * * *  webapp-svc  /var/www/myapp/shared/bin/run rake some:scheduled_task >> /var/www/myapp/shared/log/cron.log 2>&1
```

`bosun add` never overwrites this file on a re-run — same "leave existing
content untouched" rule it applies to `shared/.env`/`deploy.conf` — so your
edits are never clobbered.

## Why 6 fields, and why `/etc/cron.d/`, not `crontab -e`

A plain user's `crontab -e` has 5 fields (schedule + command) and is owned
by that user. `/etc/cron.d/*` files are root-owned and need a 6th field —
the user to run the command as — because one file can schedule jobs for
multiple users. Using `/etc/cron.d/<app>` instead of `webapp-svc`'s own
crontab is deliberate:

- `webapp-svc` is a `nologin` system account (see `argus-tty`'s
  `AT_WEBAPPS_SVC_USER`) — it has no interactive shell for `crontab -e` to
  work cleanly with.
- Keeping the schedule as a file under `/etc/cron.d/` keeps it next to the
  app's other generated config (systemd units, `deploy.conf`) instead of
  hidden inside `/var/spool/cron/`.

## Why `webapp-svc`, specifically

`shared/.env` (the app's secrets — `DATABASE_URL`, `SECRET_KEY_BASE`, etc.)
is `root:root` 600 with a single named-user ACL read grant for
`webapp-svc` — no group can read it, deliberately (see
[provisioning.md](provisioning.md)'s "Why a per-app `.env` file" section).
`shared/bin/run` (generated by
`bosun add` alongside the cron file) sources `deploy.conf` and
`shared/.env`, then `exec`s your command under the app's RVM-resolved
ruby/gemset. A cron job that doesn't run as `webapp-svc` calling this
wrapper either can't read the env vars at all, or has to re-implement that
loading itself — always prefer:

```
<schedule>  webapp-svc  /var/www/<app>/shared/bin/run <command> >> /var/www/<app>/shared/log/cron.log 2>&1
```

## Requirements for the file to actually run

1. **Owned by root**, mode `644` — `bosun add` already sets this.
2. **Clean filename** — lowercase letters/digits/`-`/`_` only, no dots, no
   `~`. The app name validation `bosun add` already enforces
   (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}$`) satisfies this.
3. No restart/reload needed — cron re-scans `/etc/cron.d/` on its own.

## Verifying a job actually ran

```bash
sudo -u webapp-svc /var/www/<app>/shared/bin/run rake some:scheduled_task  # run once by hand first
tail -f /var/www/<app>/shared/log/cron.log                                 # the job's own output
journalctl -u cron -f          # Debian/Ubuntu — follow live
grep CRON /var/log/syslog      # Debian/Ubuntu — history
```

# docs/ruby-version.md

# Changing an app's Ruby version

Bumping `RUBY_VERSION` in `deploy.conf` and re-running `bosun install` does
more than just install the new version — it also cleans up the old one,
safely, on a host where several apps share the same RVM install. This doc
covers the full sequence and exactly what gets removed and when.

## The sequence

```bash
vi /var/www/myapp/shared/deploy.conf   # bump RUBY_VERSION (and RUBY_GEMSET if you want a new gemset name too)
bosun install myapp                    # installs the new ruby, and removes the old one if it's safe to (see below)
bosun deploy myapp main                # next deploy runs `bundle install` under the NEW gemset, then symlinks + restarts
bosun setup myapp                      # optional — refreshes shared/.ruby-version/.ruby-gemset for RVM's cd-hook
```

**`install` alone does not finish the job.** It only gets the new Ruby
version and `bundler` ready — gemsets are scoped per Ruby version in RVM, so
`ruby-3.4.0@myapp` starts out completely empty even if `ruby-3.3.3@myapp`
already had the whole app's Gemfile installed. If you restarted Puma/Sidekiq
right after `install` and before a fresh `deploy`, they'd crash on boot —
the exec wrappers (`shared/bin/{puma,sidekiq}-exec`) correctly resolve
`RUBY_VERSION`/`RUBY_GEMSET` from `deploy.conf` at run time, so they'd try to
launch under the new Ruby, but find no gems installed there yet. `deploy` is
what actually runs `bundle install` against the real Gemfile under the new
gemset — see [provisioning.md](provisioning.md)'s "Why a per-app `.env`
file" section for how the exec wrappers resolve things at run time
generally.

## What `install` actually removes, and when

`install` compares two things every time it runs:

- `deploy.conf`'s current `RUBY_VERSION` (just loaded).
- `shared/.ruby-version` — written by `bosun setup`, so it still holds
  whatever version this app was set up under **last time**, independent of
  whatever `deploy.conf` says right now.

If they differ, that's a version bump, and `install` tries to remove the
**old** version — but only after checking every other app on the host:

```bash
for other_conf in /var/www/*/shared/deploy.conf; do
  grep -qx "RUBY_VERSION=<old-version>" "$other_conf" && echo "still needed by $other_conf"
done
```

- **Nothing else references it** → `rvm uninstall <old-version>` runs, and
  the install logs exactly that.
- **Something else still does** → the old version is left installed, with a
  warning naming exactly which app's `deploy.conf` is still using it.

This check exists because `rvm uninstall` removes a Ruby version — and
**every gemset under it, for every app** — not just the one you're
upgrading. Bosun deliberately runs multiple apps on one shared host (see the
main README); RVM rubies aren't scoped per app, so blindly uninstalling the
old version the moment one app moves off it could silently break a
completely different app that's still on it. Skipping removal (with a clear
reason in the log) is always the safe default here — this is opportunistic
cleanup, not something anything else depends on succeeding, so a skip or a
failed `rvm uninstall` (logged as a warning, not a fatal error) never fails
the rest of `install`.

## First-ever install isn't affected

A brand-new app has no `shared/.ruby-version` yet (that file is only written
by `bosun setup`, step 5 in the main walkthrough — AFTER `install`, step 4,
on a first-time setup). With nothing to compare against, `install` just
installs the requested version and skips the removal check entirely — no
version is ever "assumed old" on a first run.

## Checking what's actually installed

```bash
bosun version myapp     # this app's configured ruby/gemset, straight from deploy.conf
rvm list                # every Ruby version actually installed on this host
rvm gemset list_all     # every gemset under every installed ruby
```

# docs/standalone.md

# Standalone mode (no argus-tty)

Bosun is built around argus-tty's multi-tenant account model — developer/
deployer/admin tiers, a sudoers whitelist, a dedicated unprivileged
`webapp-svc` service account that secrets are ACL-locked to. If argus-tty
isn't installed, bosun no longer refuses to run: it falls back to a
**standalone mode** for a single operator on their own box instead. This
doc covers exactly what that mode is, what it isn't, and the tradeoff
you're accepting by using it.

## When it kicks in

By default (`BOSUN_MODE=auto`, or nothing set at all): automatically, the
moment `/usr/lib/argus-tty/lib/common.sh` isn't found — no flag to pass,
nothing to configure. argus-tty installed takes priority whenever it's
present; standalone is purely the fallback for when it isn't. Every bosun
subcommand checks for it independently (`deployment/lib/common`,
`bin/add.sh`, and `deployment/bootstrap` each do their own check), so
there's no scenario where half of bosun thinks argus-tty is installed and
half doesn't.

You can also choose explicitly, overriding auto-detection either way — see
"Switching modes with `bosun mode`" below. Both of these are real,
supported uses of that:

- Forcing standalone on a box that **has** argus-tty installed (for other
  reasons, or temporarily, without uninstalling it).
- Forcing argus-tty strictly, so bosun errors loudly instead of silently
  degrading to standalone if argus-tty ever goes missing by accident on a
  host where secret isolation matters.

## What actually changes

- **No tiers.** `require_role()` always passes — there's no
  developer/deployer/admin distinction to enforce when there's only one
  account using bosun at all.
- **No separate service account.** `AT_WEBAPPS_SVC_USER` — the account
  Puma/Sidekiq run as, and the only account with ACL read access to
  `shared/.env` — becomes **the same account that ran `sudo bosun add`**,
  not a dedicated unprivileged one. Everywhere bosun normally elevates to
  that service account (`bosun run`, the `assets:precompile` step in
  `do-release.sample`) skips the elevation entirely instead, since you're
  already that account.
- **One deploy key copy, not a distribution list.** `distribute_deploy_key`
  normally scans every admin/deployer account on the host; in standalone
  mode there's exactly one account to give a copy to.
- **A bosun-owned group**, `bosun-apps`, created automatically if it
  doesn't exist — standing in for argus-tty's `webapps` group. The
  standalone account is added to it automatically so it can run
  `install`/`setup`/`deploy`/`run` without needing `sudo` for everything,
  the same way argus-tty would have put a developer/admin account there.
- **`AT_RVM_ROOT` stays `/usr/local/rvm`** — RVM's multi-user path was
  never actually argus-tty's to provide; `bosun bootstrap` installs it
  either way.

## The tradeoff — read this before you rely on it

**This is the actual thing argus-tty mode gives you that standalone mode
doesn't: secrets stop being isolated from the deploying account.** There's
no second, unprivileged identity for `shared/.env` to be locked away from
— the one account that can run `bosun deploy` can also just read
`DATABASE_URL`/`SECRET_KEY_BASE` directly, because it's the same account
Puma/Sidekiq run as. If you add a second human to this box later, they
either share full access to the same account, or you're back to needing
argus-tty's tier model — standalone mode is for exactly one operator, not
a lighter-weight multi-user mode.

## Quick start

Nothing different from the normal walkthrough — just skip installing
argus-tty:

```bash
sudo apt install ./bosun_1.0.0_all.deb   # argus-tty not installed — standalone mode
# or: sudo add-apt-repository ppa:yadavramlaxman/bosun && sudo apt update && sudo apt install bosun
sudo bosun bootstrap                     # RVM multi-user, same as always

sudo bosun add myapp
#  [WARN] Added 'you' to 'bosun-apps' — log out and back in to pick it up...
# log out, log back in

vi /var/www/myapp/shared/deploy.conf
sudo vi /var/www/myapp/shared/.env
bosun install myapp
bosun setup myapp
bosun deploy myapp main
```

## You only set this once — `/etc/bosun.conf`

The standalone account defaults to whoever ran `sudo` (`$SUDO_USER`). The
**first** standalone command that resolves it this way — normally
`bosun bootstrap`, since that's step one in the walkthrough, or `bosun add`
if bootstrap already ran before argus-tty was removed — saves it to
`/etc/bosun.conf` automatically:

```bash
sudo bosun bootstrap
# [INFO] Saved standalone account 'you' to /etc/bosun.conf — future bosun
# commands won't need BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER set.
```

Every bosun command after that — `install`, `setup`, `deploy`, `run`,
`version`, even run directly as yourself with no `sudo` at all — reads it
from there with nothing to pass:

```bash
cat /etc/bosun.conf
# BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER=you

bosun install myapp     # just works, no env var needed
```

`/etc/bosun.conf` is created once and never overwritten automatically
(same idiom as `deploy.conf`/`shared/.env`) — edit it by hand if you ever
need to change the saved account.

## `BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER` — overriding it, or before it's ever been saved

Two cases need this set explicitly instead of relying on `/etc/bosun.conf`:
a literal root login with no `sudo` involved at all (no `$SUDO_USER` to
read, and nothing saved yet — bosun errors out clearly rather than guess),
or a CI/automation account that should use a different name than whatever
ends up in `/etc/bosun.conf`. An explicit value always wins over the saved
one, for that one invocation only:

```bash
sudo BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER=deploy bosun add myapp
BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER=deploy bosun install myapp
BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER=deploy bosun deploy myapp main
```

Whatever you pass must already exist as a real system account — bosun
checks (`id <name>`) and errors out immediately if it doesn't, rather than
half-provisioning an app around a name that resolves to nothing.

## Switching modes with `bosun mode`

```bash
bosun mode                  # show the configured AND effective mode right now
sudo bosun mode standalone  # force standalone, even if argus-tty IS installed
sudo bosun mode argus-tty   # require argus-tty — error instead of silently falling back
sudo bosun mode auto        # back to the default (use argus-tty if present, else standalone)
```

`bosun mode` (no argument) is read-only and needs no special privilege —
setting one writes to `/etc/bosun.conf`, so that needs root. It persists
the `BOSUN_MODE=` line in the same file `BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER=` already
lives in, never touching the other — switching modes doesn't lose a
standalone account you'd already saved, and saving a standalone account
later doesn't lose a mode you'd already chosen.

An explicit `BOSUN_MODE=argus-tty bosun install myapp` (or `standalone`)
for one command still overrides whatever's persisted, same precedence as
`BOSUN_STANDALONE_USER` above.

### Migrating existing apps after a switch — no re-deploy needed

Switching the host-wide mode doesn't touch anything already on disk — your
apps' code, releases, and `shared/.env` *content* are completely
unaffected. What's now stale is **who's allowed to read it**: file
ownership, the ACL grant on `shared/.env`, and the systemd units' `User=`
were all set up under the OLD mode's service account. For each existing
app:

```bash
sudo bosun add myapp    # idempotent — re-applies ownership/ACL/unit files
                         # for the mode you just switched to; leaves code,
                         # deploy.conf values, and shared/.env CONTENT alone
bosun restart myapp     # picks up the new systemd User= for puma/sidekiq
```

Re-running `add` here does one thing worth knowing about: it checks every
named-user entry on `shared/.env`'s ACL and strips any that aren't the
*current* `AT_WEBAPPS_SVC_USER` — so moving from argus-tty's `webapp-svc`
to a standalone account's name (or back) actually revokes the old
account's standing read access, not just adds the new one alongside it.

**One thing switching can't undo:** if you were in standalone mode, that
one account already had `shared/.env` readable directly (that's the whole
tradeoff — see above). Moving to argus-tty mode locks it down going
forward, but doesn't erase the fact that account could already read
`SECRET_KEY_BASE`/`DATABASE_URL`. Treat a standalone-to-argus-tty move as a
signal to rotate those if this box is going from single- to
multi-operator.

# docs/nginx.md

# Reverse-proxying an app with nginx

bosun does not install, configure, or manage nginx — this is a
documentation-only reference for the reverse-proxy config most Puma
deployments pair with it, pointing at the Unix socket `bosun add`/
`config/puma.rb` already create. TLS/certificate management is left
entirely to your own tooling (certbot, an internal CA, a load balancer in
front of this box, etc.) — not covered here.

> **Standalone mode (no argus-tty):** the socket is owned by your own
> account and `bosun-apps`, not literally `webapp-svc`/`webapps` — see
> [standalone.md](standalone.md). Nothing about the nginx config below
> changes either way.

## The socket bosun already gives you

Puma binds a Unix socket at:

```
/var/www/<app>/shared/tmp/sockets/puma.sock
```

(created by `deployment/setup`, see `mkdir -p
"$SHARED_PATH/tmp/sockets"`). `webapp-svc` owns it, group `webapps` — the
same account/group that already own everything else under the app tree.

## A per-app server block

One `server {}` block per app, named after the app so it's easy to keep
track of as you add more:

```nginx
# /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp
upstream myapp_puma {
  server unix:/var/www/myapp/shared/tmp/sockets/puma.sock fail_timeout=0;
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name myapp.example.com;

  # Serve precompiled assets directly, bypass Puma entirely for them.
  location ~ ^/(assets|packs)/ {
    root /var/www/myapp/current/public;
    expires max;
    add_header Cache-Control "public";
  }

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://myapp_puma;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
  }

  client_max_body_size 20m;
}
```

```bash
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/myapp /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/myapp
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx
```

## Notes

- The socket path only exists once the app has had at least one
  `bosun deploy` (actually, the socket itself is created by Puma when it
  starts under `puma-<app>.service` — the parent directory is created by
  `bosun setup`). Starting nginx before the service has ever run is fine
  — nginx returns 502 until the socket exists, same as any proxied
  upstream that isn't up yet.
- If you add `puma-app_name.socket.sample` (socket activation — see
  `docs/systemd.md`), the socket path and ownership stay the same; only
  *who creates the file* changes (systemd instead of Puma).
- TLS, rate limiting, and any WAF/CDN layer are entirely outside bosun's
  scope — this file only documents the minimum reverse-proxy wiring to the
  socket bosun already manages.
